## The problem {#sec-crm-brief}

::: {.callout-note}
## About this specification
The specification below is **my own restatement** of the project
requirements, written for this handbook; it does not reproduce the course
material. Where the requirements leave room for interpretation, the choices are
mine and are stated in @sec-crm-design.
:::

**Context.** In many insurance companies, what is known about a customer is
scattered: personal data in one program, the appointments of the sales agents
in paper diaries or spreadsheets, the signed contracts in yet another archive.
Nobody has the whole picture of a customer, and service suffers. A **customer
relationship management** (CRM) system brings these pieces together. The goal
here is a **lightweight prototype**: an interactive console application in
**C++** that manages customers and their interactions with the company in one
place. It will be the base of a real product, so a **solid, extensible
structure** matters more than features.

**What the prototype must do.**

- **R1 — Console application in C++** driven by a **main menu** of numbered
  options.
- **R2 — Add** a customer.
- **R3 — List** all customers.
- **R4 — Edit** the data of an existing customer.
- **R5 — Delete** a customer.
- **R6 — Search** customers by first name or by last name.
- **R7 — Interactions**: for each customer, add, list and search its
  interactions, which come in two kinds: **appointments** arranged by the sales
  agents and **contracts** signed by the customer.
- **R8 — Persistence**: customers and interactions are saved to text files
  (e.g. CSV) and loaded automatically when the program starts.
- **R9 — Object-oriented design**: well-designed classes with separate
  responsibilities and encapsulated data.
- **R10 — A suitable data structure** for customers, interactions, and the
  links between them.
- **R11 — A simple, robust interface**: the users are agency staff, not
  programmers, so wrong input must never crash the program.
- **R12 — Deliverable**: the source code, a short README explaining how to
  build and run the program, and a sample data file with a few customers and
  interactions to try it at once.

## Design {#sec-crm-design}

### Responsibilities

Following the single-responsibility principle (@sec-solid) and the lesson of
Part I's project (@sec-project-design), the program is split into components
that each have one reason to change:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "Architecture of the CRM. Arrows are dependencies; the graph is acyclic and the domain (Crm, Customer, Interaction) depends neither on the user interface nor on the file format."
flowchart LR
    MAIN["main.cpp<br/>(wiring)"] --> UI["ConsoleUi<br/>(menus, validated input)"]
    MAIN --> STORE["CsvStorage<br/>(file format, load/save)"]
    UI --> CRM["Crm<br/>(customers by id, search)"]
    UI --> STORE
    STORE --> CRM
    CRM --> CUST["Customer<br/>(personal data + interactions)"]
    CUST --> INT["Interaction<br/>(abstract)"]
    APP["Appointment"] --> INT
    CON["Contract"] --> INT
```

- **`Interaction`** (abstract), **`Appointment`**, **`Contract`** — what
  happened between the company and a customer (R7).
- **`Customer`** — personal data, validated, and the customer's interactions,
  which it **owns**.
- **`Crm`** — the collection: unique ids, lookup, search, sorted listing. No
  input or output.
- **`CsvStorage`** — the only component that knows the file format
  (information hiding, @sec-modularity).
- **`ConsoleUi`** — the only component that talks to the user; it reads from
  and writes to *any* pair of streams, so tests can drive it.
- **`main`** — creates the objects, loads, runs the interface, saves.

### The class hierarchy

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "UML class diagram of the domain. A Customer owns (filled diamond) any number of Interactions through std::unique_ptr; Appointment and Contract override the pure virtual functions of Interaction."
classDiagram
    class Crm {
      -customers_ : map~uint32, Customer~
      +add_customer(data) uint32
      +remove_customer(id) bool
      +find(id) Customer* or null
      +search(text) vector~const Customer*~
      +customers() vector~const Customer*~
    }
    class Customer {
      -id_ : uint32
      -data_ : CustomerData
      -interactions_ : vector~unique_ptr~Interaction~~
      +update(data)
      +add_interaction(i)
      +find_interactions(text)
      +validate(data)$ CustomerData
    }
    class Interaction {
      <<abstract>>
      -id_ : uint32
      -date_ : Date
      -notes_ : string
      +kind()* string
      +details()* string
      +matches(text) bool
      +to_record() Record
      #add_fields(record)*
    }
    class Appointment {
      -time_ : TimeOfDay
      -agent_ : string
      -place_ : string
    }
    class Contract {
      -policy_number_ : string
      -product_ : Product
      -premium_cents_ : int64
      -end_date_ : Date
    }
    Crm "1" *-- "many" Customer
    Customer "1" *-- "many" Interaction
    Interaction <|-- Appointment
    Interaction <|-- Contract
```

`Interaction` uses the **template method** pattern [@gamma1994]: the
non-virtual `to_record()` writes the fields common to all interactions and then
calls the pure virtual `add_fields()`, which each subclass implements for its
own fields. The rest of the program — listing, searching, saving — only uses
the base class interface, polymorphically (@sec-virtual).

### What is stored

The brief leaves the content of the records open; these are my assumptions,
the kind of questions one would confirm with the business:

| Entity | Fields | Rules (class invariants) |
|---|---|---|
| customer | id, first name, last name, phone, e-mail, city | names required; phone: digits, spaces, `+ - /`, at least 6 digits; e-mail: one `@` followed by a dot; no line breaks |
| appointment | id, date, time, agent, place, notes | valid date and time; agent required |
| contract | id, signing date, policy number, product (car, home, life, health, other), annual premium, end date, notes | policy number required and unique; premium $> 0$; end date after signing date |

: Data model {#tbl-crm-data}

Amounts are stored as **integer cents** (`std::int64_t`), never as `double`
(@sec-c-floats); dates are validated calendar dates in ISO 8601 form
(`YYYY-MM-DD`), which sorts correctly as text and as a `Date` object (the
defaulted `<=>` of @sec-operator-overloading compares year, month, day in that
order). Every class establishes its invariant in its constructor and throws
`std::invalid_argument` otherwise (@sec-ctors), so an invalid customer or
contract **cannot exist** in memory.

### Data structures and their costs {#sec-crm-structures}

Requirement R10 asks for a structure that also represents the **links** between
customers and interactions. The design:

- customers in a **`std::map<std::uint32_t, Customer>`** keyed by a unique id;
- each `Customer` owns its interactions in a
  **`std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Interaction>>`**, kept sorted by date;
- interaction ids are unique in the whole CRM.

The link customer → interactions is **ownership** (deleting a customer destroys
its interactions automatically, by RAII, @sec-raii); the link interaction →
customer exists only in the file, as the `customer_id` column. Ids, rather than
pointers or positions, are what the user types and what the files store: they
are stable across insertions and deletions (@sec-invalidation) and across
program runs. With $n$ customers, $k$ interactions for the customer at hand, and
names of bounded length:

| Operation | Cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| find a customer by id (edit, delete, open interactions) | $O(\log n)$ | red–black tree (@thm-red-black-height) |
| add a customer | $O(\log n)$ | map insertion |
| delete a customer | $O(\log n + k)$ | map erase + destruction of its interactions |
| list customers sorted by name | $O(n \log n)$ | `std::sort` with a strict weak order (@thm-strict-weak) |
| search by name | $O(n)$ | substring test on every customer |
| add an interaction | $O(\log k + k)$ | binary search for the position + vector insertion |
| list / search interactions of a customer | $O(k)$ | linear scan |

: Costs of the CRM operations {#tbl-crm-costs}

For an agency with a few thousand customers every operation takes microseconds,
so — as in Part I (@sec-project-design) — the decisive arguments are
**clarity** and **stability of references**, not speed. An `std::unordered_map`
would make lookups $O(1)$ expected, but the ordered map also gives files and
listings a predictable order for free.

### File format and robustness

Two CSV files with a header line (@sec-csv-cpp): `customers.csv` and
`interactions.csv`. Interactions of every kind share one table with a fixed set
of columns; the columns that do not apply to a kind stay empty. This keeps the
file readable in a spreadsheet and lets new kinds add columns without breaking
old files. Loading follows the robust pattern of @sec-report-example:

- **no files** → first run, empty CRM (not an error);
- a line with the wrong number of fields or an invalid value → **skipped**,
  with a warning naming file and line on **standard error**; the rest is
  loaded;
- if anything was skipped, the original files are copied to `*.bak` before the
  first save, so a damaged file never causes silent data loss;
- saving is **atomic**: each file is written to a temporary file and then
  renamed over the old one (@sec-atomic-writes), so a crash during a save never
  leaves a half-written file;
- data are saved **after every change** and once more at exit.

On the user side (R11), every answer goes through `std::getline` and a
validating parser (@sec-cpp-input) in a loop that re-asks with an explanation;
choosing an option by id is preceded by a list that shows the ids; deletions
ask for confirmation; and **end of input** (Ctrl+D, Ctrl+Z, the end of a
script) is turned into an `InputClosed` exception that unwinds to the main loop,
which ends the program normally — after which `main` saves. Nothing can leave
the program half-way through an operation with unsaved or inconsistent data.

### Extensibility

The brief stresses that the prototype is the base of a product. Two examples
of changes and their cost in this design:

- **a new kind of interaction** (say, a *claim*): one new class derived from
  `Interaction`, one branch in `interaction_from_record`, its columns in the
  storage, and a menu entry. Listing, searching and deleting work unchanged —
  the open–closed principle (@sec-solid);
- **a different storage** (a database instead of CSV files): a new class with
  `load` and `save`; neither the domain nor the interface changes.

### Building

The project is built exactly as the README says, here with the strictest
settings of @sec-flags: warnings as errors and AddressSanitizer plus
UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, so that any memory error or leak during the
demonstration and the tests would stop the program with a report.

```{python}

   "-DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer' > /dev/null && "
   "cmake --build build | tail -3")
```

## Demonstration {#sec-crm-demo}

To make the demonstration reproducible we do not type at a keyboard: a Python
script starts the compiled program with `subprocess.run`, writes a scripted
session to its standard input, and collects its output and exit status —
the technique of @sec-subprocess-run. The `--echo` option makes the program
repeat each input line, so the output reads like a real session. The first
session starts from the sample data and makes several deliberate mistakes.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import shutil, subprocess
DATA = WORK / "demo-data"                         # a fresh copy of the sample data
shutil.rmtree(DATA, ignore_errors=True)
shutil.copytree(WORK / "data", DATA)

def crm_session(lines, show_from=0):
    """Run the CRM on scripted input; print its output (from a given line) and exit status."""
    result = subprocess.run([str(WORK / "build" / "crm"), str(DATA), "--echo"],
                            input="".join(l + "\n" for l in lines),
                            capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
    out = result.stdout.replace(str(DATA), "demo-data")
    print("\n".join(out.splitlines()[show_from:]))
    if result.stderr:
        print("--- standard error ---\n" + result.stderr.replace(str(DATA), "demo-data"))
    print("--- exit status:", result.returncode)

session_1 = [
    "7", "abc",                                          # invalid menu choices
    "2", "Elena", "", "Marino", "12ab", "+39 06 5550 9876", "elena@", "elena.marino@example.it", "Roma",
    "6", "99", "5",                                      # unknown customer id, then Elena (id 5)
    "2", "2026-11-31", "2026-11-25", "9.30", "09:30", "", "Sara Conti", "Roma Eur agency", "Quote for a home policy",
    "3", "CAR-2026-0007", "HOME-2026-0141", "house", "home", "2026-12-01", "2026-11-30", "2027-11-30",
    "-100", "312,40", "",
    "1", "0",                                            # list Elena's interactions, back
    "3", "MAR",                                          # search: Marino (last name), Marco (first name)
    "0",
]
crm_session(session_1)
```

Every mistake was caught with an explanation and a new prompt: menu choices out
of range or not numbers, an empty last name, a phone with letters, an
incomplete e-mail, an unknown customer id, 31 November, a time without the
colon, an empty agent, a policy number that already belongs to another
customer, an unknown product, an end date before the signing date, a negative
premium. The amount `312,40` with a decimal comma was accepted. The search for
`MAR` matched *Marino* and *Marco* — first and last names, case-insensitively
(R6).

The second session reloads the data saved by the first, edits a customer
(keeping some fields with Enter and clearing one with `-`), searches
interactions, deletes a customer with all its interactions, and then the input
**ends abruptly**, in the middle of the main menu, as if the user had pressed
Ctrl+D. We show only the part after loading and the first menu:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
session_2 = [
    "4", "2", "", "", "-", "marco.russo@example.com", "",      # edit Marco Russo
    "6", "1", "4", "car", "0",                                  # Giulia Ferrari: search "car"
    "5", "3", "maybe", "y",                                     # delete Chiara Esposito (after an invalid answer)
    "1",                                                        # list, then the input ends
]
crm_session(session_2, show_from=10)
```

The program reported end of input, saved and exited with status 0 (R11). The
files on disk now contain the changes of both sessions; quoting protects the
note containing a comma (R8):

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
print((DATA / "customers.csv").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print((DATA / "interactions.csv").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
```

Customer 3 and its life-insurance contract are gone; Elena Marino (id 5) has
an appointment and a contract with new interaction ids 6 and 7; Marco Russo's
phone was cleared and his e-mail added.

## Tests {#sec-crm-tests}

### Unit tests in C++

`tests/tests.cpp` checks the parts of the program in isolation — text
utilities, dates, invariants of every class, the `Crm` operations, a
save/load round trip with commas and quotes in the data, the handling of damaged
lines, and the user interface driven by an `std::istringstream` (including
input that ends in the middle of a form). It uses no testing library: a
`CHECK` macro counts failures, and the program's exit status tells `ctest` or a
CI system whether everything passed (@sec-filter).

```{python}
show_file("tests/tests.cpp")
sh("cd crm && ./build/crm_tests && echo \"exit status: $?\"")
```

All checks pass under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, which
also verified that no memory leaks at exit.

### End-to-end tests from Python

The Python side checks the behaviours that only the complete program shows:
exit statuses, files on disk, messages on standard error.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: true
import tempfile

def run_crm(folder, lines, *extra_args):
    return subprocess.run([str(WORK / "build" / "crm"), str(folder), *extra_args],
                          input="".join(l + "\n" for l in lines),
                          capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)

tests = {}
tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())

# First run in an empty folder: no crash, files created with only the headers.
r = run_crm(tmp / "new", ["0"])
tests["first run: status 0"] = r.returncode == 0 and "empty CRM" in r.stdout
tests["first run: files created"] = (tmp / "new" / "customers.csv").read_text().startswith("id,first_name")

# Wrong usage: status 2 and a message on stderr.
r = run_crm(tmp / "new", ["0"], "--verbose")
tests["wrong option: status 2"] = r.returncode == 2 and "usage" in r.stderr

# Damaged data: bad lines skipped with line numbers, good ones kept, backup made.
bad = tmp / "bad"; bad.mkdir()
shutil.copy(WORK / "data" / "interactions.csv", bad)
(bad / "customers.csv").write_text(
    "id,first_name,last_name,phone,email,city\n"
    "1,Giulia,Ferrari,,,Milano\n"
    "2,Marco,,,,Torino\n"                       # empty last name -> invalid
    "3,\"Chiara,Esposito,,,Napoli\n"            # unterminated quote
    "4,Luca,Bianchi,,,Bologna\n", encoding="utf-8")
r = run_crm(bad, ["0"])
damaged_report = r.stderr
tests["damaged: still status 0"] = r.returncode == 0
tests["damaged: 2 customers loaded"] = "Loaded 2 customer(s)" in r.stdout
tests["damaged: warnings with line numbers"] = "customers.csv line 3" in r.stderr and "line 4" in r.stderr
tests["damaged: interactions of skipped customers reported"] = "unknown customer 2" in r.stderr
tests["damaged: backup kept"] = (bad / "customers.csv.bak").exists()
tests["second run on the saved files: no warnings"] = run_crm(bad, ["0"]).stderr == ""

# End of input while typing a new customer: nothing half-added, data saved, status 0.
r = run_crm(tmp / "new", ["2", "Grace"])
tests["eof mid-form: status 0, nothing added"] = (r.returncode == 0 and
    (tmp / "new" / "customers.csv").read_text().count("\n") == 1)

for name, ok in tests.items():
    print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {name}")
print(f"{sum(tests.values())}/{len(tests)} end-to-end tests passed")
print("--- standard error of the run on the damaged files ---")
print(damaged_report.strip())
```

Note the consequence of the design checked by the second-to-last test: after
the run on the damaged files, the CRM saved only what it could read — the
originals are preserved in `*.bak` for a human to inspect — so the next run
starts clean.

### How the reference implementation meets the requirements

| Requirement | Where |
|---|---|
| R1 menu-driven C++ console program | `ConsoleUi::run`, `interactions_menu` (menu loops with `switch`) |
| R2–R5 add, list, edit, delete customers | `ConsoleUi::add_customer`, `list_customers`, `edit_customer`, `delete_customer`; `Crm` |
| R6 search by first or last name | `Crm::search` (case-insensitive substring, sorted result) |
| R7 appointments and contracts: add, list, search | `Interaction` hierarchy; `Customer::add_interaction`, `find_interactions`; sub-menu |
| R8 CSV persistence, automatic loading | `CsvStorage::load` at start, `save` after each change and at exit; atomic writes, backups |
| R9 OOP with encapsulation | private data, validating constructors, `const` accessors, abstract base, rule of zero |
| R10 data structure with links | `std::map<id, Customer>`, owned `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Interaction>>`, global ids (@tbl-crm-costs) |
| R11 robust interface | `read_line` + validators, `InputClosed`, confirmations; tested in C++ and from Python |
| R12 sources, README, sample data | `cpp/_crm`: CMake project, `README.md`, `data/` |

## Extensions {#sec-crm-extensions}

1. **A third kind of interaction.** Add `Claim` (date of the event, amount
   requested, status: open/accepted/rejected) as described in
   @sec-crm-design, with tests. Count how many existing lines you had to
   change.
2. **Reminders.** List the contracts that expire in the next 30 days, across
   all customers, sorted by end date. Which data structure would make this
   $O(\log n + m)$ for $m$ results? (Hint: an ordered index such as
   `std::multimap<Date, id>`, kept up to date.)
3. **Undo.** Keep a stack of inverse operations and add an *undo* option, as
   suggested for Part I (@sec-project-extensions).
4. **Unicode-aware search.** `to_lower` only folds ASCII letters, so searching
   `élena` does not find `Élena`. Find out what Unicode case folding is and
   which library (e.g. ICU) provides it.
5. **A Python report tool.** Write a Python script that reads the two CSV
   files with the `csv` module (@sec-csv) and produces, with pandas, the total
   annual premium per product and per city. Because the file format is
   documented, the two programs cooperate without sharing any code.
6. **A batch mode.** Add command-line options such as
   `crm data --export-json` that print the whole CRM as JSON lines on standard
   output and exit, so that other programs can consume it through a pipe
   (@sec-ch-cpp-python).
7. **SQLite storage.** Implement a `SqliteStorage` with the same `load`/`save`
   interface, extract an abstract base class `Storage`, and switch backends with
   a command-line option.
